pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Magnetic Poles

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** England DfE KS2 Year 3 'Forces and magnets' — 'describe magnets as having 2 poles; predict whether 2 magnets will attract or repel each other, depending on which poles are facing';

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS 3-PS2-3 (cause-and-effect: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-3]).

- **Operational details:** Best practice builds the rule from repeated predict-then-test trials with two labelled magnets, using precise pole language.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 7-9). The goal is a predictive RULE grounded in observation — every magnet has two poles (north-seeking/south-seeking); like poles repel, opposite poles attract; predict the outcome of bringing two magnets together from how their poles face. NO field model or explanation of WHY yet (that is KS3).
bestPractices: Build the rule empirically: child orients two labelled bar magnets, predicts attract or repel, then tests — across enough trials the pattern 'like repel, opposite attract' emerges as their own discovery.

Use precise, consistent pole language — 'north-seeking' and 'south-seeking' (a freely-moving magnet's north-seeking pole points north) — then progress to 'north pole'/'south pole' as understanding consolidates (IOP Spark progression).
Colour-code and label the poles (e.g. N red / S blue) so orientation is unambiguous while children are still learning the rule.

Confront the repulsion case explicitly and often — children adopt repulsion of like poles much more slowly than attraction of opposites, so give plentiful like-pole trials and the felt 'invisible push'.
Show magnets of different shapes (bar, ring, button, horseshoe) so pupils learn poles are a property of every magnet, not 'the two ends of a bar'.
keyRepresentations: Two colour-coded bar magnets (N/S labelled) brought together in the four orientations: N-N, S-S (repel) and N-S, S-N (attract)
A predict-then-test record table: orientation drawn → prediction → observed outcome
The 'like repel, opposite attract' rule stated as a short, memorable line
A freely-suspended/floating magnet swinging to point north (anchors the 'north-seeking' name)
commonMisconceptions: Children are slow to adopt the idea of poles and only gradually come to see magnetic effects as attraction of unlike poles and repulsion of like poles (IOP Spark) — repulsion is grasped later than attraction.
Reversing the rule (thinking like poles attract) — hence the need for many disconfirming like-pole trials.
Thinking poles are always 'the two ends' — not true for ring/button magnets; poles are a property of every magnet whatever its shape.
Thinking any two magnets always just 'stick' — ignoring that orientation determines attract vs repel.
Assuming a bigger magnet is automatically the stronger one (carried over from the materials topic).

learn.summary: For children aged 7-9, build the rule 'like poles repel, opposite poles attract' from repeated predict-then-test trials with two labelled magnets. The target is a predictive rule grounded in observation: every magnet has two poles (north-seeking/south-seeking); predict whether two magnets attract or repel from how their poles face. No field model or explanation of why yet. Repulsion of like poles is grasped more slowly than attraction of opposites, so give plentiful like-pole trials. Poles are a property of every magnet, whatever its shape.

activities.title: Predict-then-test with two labelled magnets
feedback: When two like poles (e.g. two north ends) face, you feel them resist and push apart, and the push gets stronger the closer you bring them. That is repulsion, and it surprises many people because we often assume magnets always stick.
When opposite poles face (north and south), they snap together — attraction.
If you flip one magnet and the outcome changes from repel to attract with the same pair, that shows the pole orientation decides the result, not the push or the particular magnets.
If you predicted they would always stick, try the like-pole case again and pay attention to the felt push — magnets do not always attract.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is a predictive rule about orientation. Letting the child set the orientation and immediately feel/see the consequence (snap or spring-apart), then flip one pole to reverse the outcome, makes the cause unmistakable and matches the predict-then-test loop the curriculum asks for.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: describe magnets as having 2 poles, and predict whether 2 magnets will attract or repel depending on which poles are facing.
3-PS2-3 cause-and-effect example: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-3] (objects not in contact).
learnerActions: Take two bar magnets with poles colour-coded and labelled (e.g. north red, south blue).
Set an orientation by bringing two ends toward each other; before pushing, say aloud your prediction: will they attract or repel?
Slowly push them together and observe/feel what happens: do they snap together, or meet an invisible springy resistance that pushes them apart unless you force them?
Work through all four orientations: N-N, S-S, N-S, S-N. Record each in a table: draw the orientation, write your prediction, write what actually happened.
On one pair that repels (e.g. N-N), flip just ONE magnet and push again — notice the outcome reverses.
After enough trials, state the pattern you discovered in your own short rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether two magnets attract or repel depends on which poles face each other: like poles push apart, opposite poles pull together. Because flipping one magnet reverses the outcome with the SAME pair, the result depends on which poles face each other, not on which particular magnets you use.

activities.title: Confront the repulsion case head-on
feedback: Feeling the push with your own hands, or watching the ends spring apart, is direct evidence that 'magnets always attract' is incomplete.
If you can predict repulsion before you push for like poles, you have grasped the harder half of the rule.
activities.rationale: Research reviews note children adopt repulsion of like poles more slowly than attraction of opposites, so plentiful disconfirming like-pole trials, and observing/feeling the push, are needed.
sourceClaims: Students are slow to adopt the idea of magnetic poles and only gradually come to see magnetic effects in terms of attraction of unlike poles and repulsion of like poles.
learnerActions: Spend extra trials on like-pole orientations (N-N and S-S), slowly pushing and feeling the resistance.
Describe the sensation: an invisible springy wall that slides and bounces and pushes the ends apart unless you force them together.
Predict the like-pole outcome ahead of each push, then test, until you reliably expect repulsion.
activities.intendedInsight: Two magnets can push each other away. Repulsion is just as real as attraction and happens specifically when like poles face.

activities.title: Poles on magnets of every shape
feedback: If you thought a ring or horseshoe magnet has no poles, locating them with filings or another magnet shows otherwise, and testing with a labelled magnet tells you which pole is north and which is south.
Finding that the attract/repel behaviour still depends on which pole you present confirms the rule holds for any shape.
activities.rationale: Addresses the misconception that poles are always at the ends; using differently shaped magnets shows poles are a general property.
sourceClaims: Use full pole names (north-seeking/south-seeking) to consolidate understanding, progressing to north/south pole; address the misconceptions that all magnets look the same and that poles are always at the ends, via differently shaped magnets.
learnerActions: Examine magnets of different shapes: bar, ring, button, horseshoe.

For a horseshoe or ring magnet, find where the poles are using iron filings (they cluster at the poles but cannot tell you which is north and which is south), then test with a labelled magnet to name each pole: the part that repels the labelled north pole is a north pole. Ring and button magnets often have their poles on the flat faces rather than at the ends.
State where the north and south poles are on each magnet — not just on the two ends of a bar.
activities.intendedInsight: Every magnet has a north and a south pole whatever its shape; poles are a property of the whole magnet, not simply 'the two ends of a bar'.

activities.title: Name the poles: the north-seeking anchor
feedback: If the freely-turning magnet (on a thread or on its float) always settles pointing the same way, that is the north-seeking pole revealing itself.
Using consistent names for the poles makes your attract/repel predictions clearer.
activities.rationale: Precise, consistent pole language supports the rule; naming can serve as a vocabulary/reference layer alongside the hands-on trials.
sourceClaims: Use full pole names (north-seeking/south-seeking) to consolidate understanding, progressing to north/south pole; address the misconceptions that all magnets look the same and that poles are always at the ends, via differently shaped magnets.
learnerActions: Let a single magnet turn freely: suspend it on a thread, or rest it on a small float (e.g. a cork or foam disc) on water, and watch it swing until it settles.
Keeping it away from other magnets and steel objects, notice which end points roughly north; name that end the 'north-seeking' pole and the other the 'south-seeking' pole.
Use this precise language ('north-seeking'/'south-seeking', progressing to 'north pole'/'south pole') when describing your predict-then-test trials.
activities.intendedInsight: A freely-moving magnet's north-seeking pole points north, which is where the name comes from. Consistent pole language keeps orientation unambiguous.

activities.title: Retrieval practice: predict the outcome
feedback: Correct: like poles (N-N, S-S) repel; opposite poles (N-S, S-N) attract.
If a question flips one magnet, the outcome switches — check your answer reflects that the orientation changed.
Make sure like-pole items are answered as 'repel', since children often learn that case more slowly.
activities.rationale: Prediction, matching and categorising orientations give a precise, direct test of the rule and strong retrieval practice. This checks and consolidates the rule rather than discovering it, so it works best after the hands-on trials. A sorting/matching task can check classification of orientations but does not itself elicit the felt repulsion or an explanation.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: describe magnets as having 2 poles, and predict whether 2 magnets will attract or repel depending on which poles are facing.
learnerActions: Given a diagram of two magnets in a stated orientation (e.g. 'north facing north'), decide: attract or repel?
Match orientation diagrams to their outcomes.
Sort a set of orientations into two groups: those that attract and those that repel.
Answer transfer items: 'If a magnet is flipped, what changes?' and 'Where are the poles on this horseshoe?'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule can be applied reliably to new orientations, including the slower-learned like-pole (repel) cases and flipped magnets.

constraints: Keep to Tier A (concrete/observational): the goal is a predictive rule from observation. Do not introduce a magnetic field model or an explanation of WHY poles attract/repel — that is later (KS3) material.
Colour-code and label the poles (e.g. N red / S blue) while the rule is still being learned, so orientation is unambiguous.
Give plentiful like-pole trials: repulsion of like poles is learned later than attraction, so do not under-represent it.
Retrieval-practice items check and consolidate the rule but do not let the child discover it or feel the repulsion; use them after hands-on predict-then-test work, not instead of it.

A naming/reference layer (tappable labels, lift-the-flap answers) supports vocabulary but states the rule rather than letting orientation be manipulated; pair it with manipulation rather than relying on it alone.
Watch for the carried-over idea that a bigger magnet is automatically stronger — size is not the subject of this rule.
Use classroom-grade magnets with normal supervision; avoid strong rare-earth magnets that can pinch or shatter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 3D-interactive artefact 'poor', asserting depth/viewpoint 'add nothing' and that a static image 'cannot' give live recompute. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped. A static representation can still teach the rule by presenting labelled orientations, and a 3D model would simply offer a different experience. The affordance worth keeping is that live re-evaluation as a magnet rotates can make the orientation-to-outcome link vivid — offered as a helpful option, not a necessity.
The source also rated an in-role 'conversation' format poor; this is a fit judgement, not evidence that dialogue cannot support the topic, so it is not asserted as a universal limit.

One source (Oak National Academy) is marked verified:false in the row; its claims about pole-naming progression and shape-based misconceptions are used as pedagogical guidance, not as established efficacy.

Physical bar/ring/horseshoe magnets are safe for this age with normal supervision; strong rare-earth magnets can pinch or shatter — this practical caution was not in the source and is flagged for review, not asserted as sourced.

The claim that feeling/seeing repulsion is the decisive evidence reflects a preferred scaffold (hands-on predict-then-test); it is not asserted that touch is uniquely required, and seeing the ends spring apart serves the same observable purpose.

The free-turning magnet demonstration was corrected: a magnet sinks if placed directly on water, so the activity now specifies suspending it on a thread or resting it on a cork/foam float. This practical detail is a standard classroom method, not a sourced specification.

assess.poeTask: Hand the child two bar magnets with poles marked. Ask them to predict what happens as two same-coloured ends approach, and WHY, before pushing them together — then repeat with opposite ends. Feeling like poles REPEL is the surprise that breaks 'magnets always attract'; the pre-push reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Now I flip ONE magnet so a red end faces a blue end. What happens now, and why is it different?
Can two magnets ever PUSH each other away? When?
Where are the poles on this horseshoe magnet — does it even have them?
assess.correctAnswer: They push apart / you feel them resist — they repel. Two like poles (north and north) repel each other; only opposite poles (north and south) attract. So facing two norths together makes them push away.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They'll snap together — magnets always attract each other.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give plentiful like-pole trials so the child FEELS the repulsion; label the poles and state the rule.
errorPatterns.distractor: They'll pull together and stick — magnets always attract.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts attraction regardless of which poles face each other.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A magnet only has poles if it's a straight bar with two ends — a ring or horseshoe magnet doesn't have them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that every magnet has a north and a south pole whatever its shape; locate them with iron filings or another magnet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't locate poles on a horseshoe or ring magnet.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Whether they attract or repel is random, or about how hard you push them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the poles and show that flipping ONE magnet reliably switches attract to repel and back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't attribute the outcome to the pole orientation.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts the magnets always attract/stick whatever the ends; treats repulsion as impossible or as something random.
responseLevels.full: Predicts attraction or repulsion from the pole orientation, explains it by like/opposite poles, transfers correctly when a magnet is flipped, and recognises every magnet has two poles whatever its shape.
responseLevels.partial: States 'like poles repel, opposite poles attract' and may predict the like-pole case, but recites the rule without linking the outcome to WHICH poles face — e.g. can't predict reliably after a magnet is flipped, or thinks only bar ends have poles.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I have two bar magnets. I turn them so their two RED (north) ends face each other and slowly push them together. What will happen as they get close — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Children learn 'magnets attract' long before they accept that two magnets can PUSH APART. A child who only holds 'magnets stick together' predicts they snap together whatever the ends. A child with the pole rule predicts repulsion for like poles and, in tier 2, refers to the two SAME poles — not just 'magnets attract'. Facing like poles is the case that separates the rule from the everyday 'magnets stick' idea.
